title: Easy exam 8
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: password files, GRUB, pipes, tests, command substitution, process states, pagers, links and inodes.

options.t: It holds the hashed passwords and ordinary users cannot read it.
options.why: Its mode is `-rw-r----- root shadow`: only root and the group `shadow` can read it.

options.t: It holds the passwords in plain text, so root can tell them to users who forget them.
options.why: Only a one-way hash is stored; nobody can read the password back from it.

options.t: It is readable by everybody, because every login has to consult it.
options.why: The login program runs as root. The world-readable file is `/etc/passwd`, which holds no hashes.

options.t: It lists the home directory and the login shell of every user.
options.why: Those fields are in `/etc/passwd`.

questions.title: Changing the GRUB menu
questions.text: On a Debian-like system you want a longer menu timeout in GRUB. Which procedure is right?

options.t: Edit `/etc/default/grub` and then run `update-grub`, which regenerates `/boot/grub/grub.cfg`.
options.why: `grub.cfg` is generated from the settings in `/etc/default/grub` and the scripts in `/etc/grub.d/`.

options.t: Edit `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` by hand: `update-grub` only reads it.
options.why: `update-grub` writes that file, so a manual edit is lost the next time it runs.

options.t: Edit `/etc/default/grub` and reboot: GRUB reads that file directly at boot.
options.why: GRUB reads `grub.cfg`, which only changes when `update-grub` is run.

options.t: Run `update-grub` after editing `/etc/default/grub`: that command also installs GRUB in the first sector of the disk.
options.why: Writing the boot loader to the disk is the job of `grub-install`; `update-grub` only rewrites the configuration.

questions.title: Error message in a pipe
questions.text: `/nonexistent` does not exist. What happens when you type `ls /nonexistent | wc -l`?

options.t: The error message of `ls` appears on the screen and `wc` prints `0`.
options.why: The pipe connects only stdout; the error message goes to stderr, which is still the terminal, so `wc` receives nothing.

options.t: `wc` prints `1`, because the error message is one line.
options.why: The message never reaches `wc`: it travels on stderr, not through the pipe.

options.t: Nothing appears: the message is passed to `wc`, which only prints counts.
options.why: `wc` would then print `1`; in fact the message goes straight to the terminal.

options.t: `wc` waits for input for ever, because `ls` produced no output.
options.why: `ls` ends, its stdout is closed, and `wc` sees the end of the input and prints `0`.

options.t: `[ -z "$x" ]` is true when the variable `x` is empty.
options.why: True: `-z` is true for a string of length zero.

options.t: `[ -d /tmp ]` is true when `/tmp` is a directory.
options.why: True: `-d` tests for a directory.

options.t: `[ -s notes ]` is true when `notes` exists and is not empty.
options.why: True: `-s` means "exists and has a size greater than zero".

options.t: `[ -e name ]` is true only when `name` is a regular file.
options.why: False: `-e` is true for anything that exists (file, directory, link...). The test for a regular file is `-f`.

questions.title: Saving a count in a variable
questions.text: `data.txt` has 3 lines. Which command makes `echo "$n"` print `3`?

options.t: `n=$(wc -l < data.txt)`
options.why: Command substitution replaces `$(...)` with what the command prints; with `<` the output is just the number.

options.t: `n=wc -l < data.txt`
options.why: The shell sees the assignment `n=wc` before the command `-l`: it fails with "-l: command not found".

options.t: `n='wc -l < data.txt'`
options.why: Single quotes keep the text as it is: `n` would contain the words `wc -l < data.txt`.

options.t: `n=${wc -l < data.txt}`
options.why: `${...}` is parameter expansion, not command substitution: bash answers "bad substitution".

questions.title: The T state
questions.text: You run `ps -o stat= -p 4321` and it prints `T`. What is that process doing?

options.t: It is stopped (suspended), for example after `Ctrl+Z` or a `SIGSTOP`.
options.why: `T` is the stopped state; `fg`, `bg` or `kill -CONT` make it run again.

options.t: It is running on a CPU or ready to run.
options.why: That is `R`.

options.t: It is sleeping, waiting for an event such as a read to complete.
options.why: That is `S` (interruptible sleep).

options.t: It has finished but its parent has not collected its exit status yet.
options.why: That is a zombie, shown as `Z`.

questions.title: Paging a file
questions.text: Which statement about viewing files is FALSE?

options.t: `cat file` writes the whole file at once, without pausing.
options.why: True: for a long file only the last lines stay on the screen.

options.t: `less file` lets you go back with `b` or the arrow keys and search with `/`.
options.why: True: that is what makes `less` more convenient than `more`.

options.t: `more file` shows the file one screen at a time.
options.why: True: it is the older pager.

options.t: `less` has to read the whole file before it shows the first screen.
options.why: False: `less` shows the first screen at once and loads the rest as needed, which is why it opens huge files immediately.

questions.title: Argument order of ln -s
questions.text: Which command creates a symbolic link called `latest` that points to `/var/log/syslog`?

options.t: `ln -s /var/log/syslog latest`
options.why: The order is the target first and the name of the new link second.

options.t: `ln -s latest /var/log/syslog`
options.why: It tries to create a link named `/var/log/syslog` pointing to `latest`: it fails because that file already exists.

options.t: `ln /var/log/syslog latest`
options.why: Without `-s` it makes a hard link, not a symbolic link.

options.t: `ln -s -t latest /var/log/syslog`
options.why: `-t` expects the directory in which the links are created; `latest` does not exist, so it fails.

questions.title: The inode after mv
questions.text: In one directory you run `ls -i a.txt`, then `mv a.txt b.txt`, then `ls -i b.txt`. What do the two `ls -i` print?

options.t: The same inode number both times.
options.why: `mv` inside one file system only changes the name stored in the directory entry; the inode (the file itself) is not touched.

options.t: Two different inode numbers, because `b.txt` is a new file.
options.why: No new file is created: the same inode just has another name.

options.t: The second command fails: after the `mv` there is no inode left.
options.why: The inode still exists, now reached through the name `b.txt`.

options.t: The same number, but only because `mv` leaves a hard link called `a.txt` behind.
options.why: `mv` removes the old name; nothing is left behind under `a.txt`.

questions.title: Jumping in a pager
questions.text: You are reading a long manual page with `man`. Which key takes you to the end of the page?

options.why: In `less` (the pager used by `man`) `G` goes to the last line and `g` to the first.
It goes to the beginning of the page.
It quits the pager.
It shows the help screen of the pager.
